role: Machine instructions of every bwx12 kernel, as text, written when bwx12 was built.
purpose: This file holds the machine instructions of the 55 kernel functions of the binary bwx12, as text. The build script build12.sh wrote it on CRB on 2026-11-15 with the tool objdump, in the same run that compiled bwx12 [Ref1] [Ref10].

main_flow.step: The file holds 55 blocks, one per kernel of bwx12, in the order in which the command `bwx12 --list` prints the kernel names [Ref1]. The table below shows the six kernels of bwx12 that the whole-chip test timed: `read`, `asmread`, `oldread`, `read_1pl`, `read_nop96` and `read_nop256`.
A block starts with the header `=== bwx12 <kernel> ===`.
The next line gives the start address of the function (16 hexadecimal digits) and its name `k_<kernel>`.
Each further line is one machine instruction: its address (hexadecimal), the name of the instruction, the operands. Every instruction is 4 bytes long. So the addresses rise by 4.
In the operands, a number after `#` is decimal unless it starts with `0x`. Example: `#224` is 224, and `#0x100` is 256.

A branch line shows the target address and, in angle brackets, the same target as function name plus offset. objdump adds the words after `//`: other names of the branch condition, or the decimal value of a constant.

To find the loop of a kernel, look for the branch whose target address is lower than its own address and lies inside the function. The loop is the lines from that target to the branch. Example: the branch at line 14 jumps to `49a4`. That address is line 4. So the loop of `read` is lines 4 to 14.
The instructions before the loop and after the loop run at most once per call of the kernel.
An empty line ends the block.

behavior_notes: Part L, part C and control I of the whole-chip test ran the binary that this listing describes. build.txt records the sha256 value of the binary bwx12 and of this file from the same build [Ref10]. go.sh and go2.sh stop unless bwx12 has that sha256 value [Ref11]. The binary bwx12 is not in the local folders. Its sha256 value is known only from records such as build.txt, go.sh and go2.sh. On 2026-11-21 the copy of this file in this folder had the sha256 value that build.txt records (checked with `sha256sum`). On the same day the copy of bwx12.c in the parent folder had the sha256 value that build.txt records for the source.

Part A did not run bwx12. It ran the binaries bw_old and bw_new [Ref16]. In each of the two it timed six kernels: `read`, `write`, `copy`, `asmread`, `asmwrite` and `asmcopy` [Ref16]. Notes below compare their read loops with this listing. The function list below describes the functions of bwx12 only. There, "Not run in the whole-chip test" means that no part of the test ran that function of bwx12.
Instructions per 256 B of buffer: `read` 11, `asmread` 11, `oldread` 32 (two loop passes of 16), `read_1pl` 7, `read_nop96` 107, `read_nop256` 267.

The old read kernel and the load-only loops use the same load instruction in the same number: 8 `ldp` of 32 B per 256 B. The old read kernel adds every loaded value to a running sum (16 vector adds per 256 B). The load-only loops use no loaded value.
`read_1pl` loads 64 B per 256 B. bwx12 counts the whole length of the range that a call covers. So the rate of `read_1pl` counts 256 B per loop pass [Ref8].

The whole-chip test runs bwx12 with `--bytes 256M` (a buffer of 256 MiB per thread) and `--stop common` [Ref9]. With `--stop common` all threads of an interval have one common deadline. One timed call of a kernel covers 2 MiB, and the thread reads the clock after each call [Ref8]. A thread ends its interval at the first clock read at or after the deadline. A call over 2 MiB runs 8192 passes of a 256 B loop, or 16384 passes of the `oldread` loop. So the instructions before and after a loop run at most once per 2 MiB.
Before each interval a thread runs one warm-up call of the kernel over its whole 256 MiB buffer. This call is not timed [Ref8].
Each thread fills its buffer once with `k_write` (lines 17 to 32, not shown below) before the first interval. This first touch is not timed [Ref8].

The machine instructions of `read`, `asmread` and `oldread` equal those of `k_read` and `k_asmread` of bw_new and of `k_read` of bw_old in the listing of 2026-11-13 [Ref14]. Only addresses and the function name `k_oldread` differ. Each of the three loops starts at the same address modulo 64 as in that listing (36, 20 and 40). A script of this task compared the texts on 2026-11-21. Method: drop the address column, replace each branch target by its distance from the function start, drop the words after `//`, then compare line by line. With this method every line of `read` and of `asmread` is equal. Three lines of `oldread` still differ: the two `adrp` lines (lines 137 and 189) and the `bl` line (line 204). They hold addresses outside the function.

Part A timed `asmread` in bw_old too [Ref16]. With the same method, every line of `k_asmread` of bw_old in the listing of 2026-11-13 equals the same line of `asmread` in this file [Ref14]. The loop of `k_asmread` of bw_old starts at address 28 modulo 64. The loops of `asmread` in bwx12 and in bw_new start at 20.

The binaries bw_old and bw_new are not in the local folders. So the comparisons above use the listing of 2026-11-13, not the binaries. The sha256 values of the two binaries are known only from records. The file of that listing holds the two values [Ref14]. ra.sh, the script of part A, stops unless bw_old and bw_new have these values [Ref16].

bwx12.c pads the code before each kernel. The pad makes the kernel start at a chosen address modulo 64 [Ref15]. offsets.tsv lists the function start, the loop start and the loop start modulo 64 of every kernel [Ref12]. Its values for the six kernels equal the addresses in the table below.

check_listing12.py compares this file with the accepted listing of bwx11 and with the expected loop of each new kernel. The saved output of this check says `ok` for all 55 kernels and counts 0 failed rows [Ref13].
The compiler was gcc 14.2.0 with the flags `-O3 -march=native -fno-tree-loop-distribute-patterns -pthread -Wall -Wextra -std=gnu11 -fno-ipa-icf -fno-toplevel-reorder -falign-functions=4` [Ref10].

words.def: the Arm reference server under test. It has 128 CPUs.
our runs use CPUs 0-119 only: 64 threads on mesh 0 plus 56 threads on mesh 1. Each thread reads its own buffer of 256 MiB from memory.
the two halves of the chip. CPUs 0-63 sit on mesh 0. CPUs 64-127 sit on mesh 1.
the inner loop of the benchmark that reads memory. On this page "kernel" means this loop. The operating system kernel is always written "Linux kernel".
portable C code with 16 running sums. Each load is followed by an add. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_old and `oldread` in the runner bwx12.
NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions), loads only. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_new and `read` in bwx12.
a hand-written load-only loop. It has the same 8 "ldp q" loads per 256 B as the new read kernel. "ldp q" is the Arm instruction that loads two 16-byte vector registers.
the new read kernel or asmread.
test loops of bwx12: the asmread loop with 96 or 256 no-operation instructions per 256 B, and a loop with one load per 64 B line.
the benchmark and its two binaries of 2026-11-13. bw_old was built from the old source, bw_new from the new source.
later runner programs for the same loops. They print one row per thread. bwx12 is the runner of the 2026-11-15 investigation. bwx11 and bwx are older versions.

a process is one start of a benchmark binary. An interval is one timed measurement inside a process. bwx12 times a sequence of kernels and repeats the sequence: each repeat is a round (counted from 0), and the position is the place of a kernel in the sequence (counted from 0). In part A the round (1 or 2) is the round of the script: round 2 runs the processes in the reverse order.
the 120-thread part of the test of 2026-11-13, repeated with the same two binaries.
one bwx12 process with the kernel sequence oldread, asmread, read_nop96, read_nop256, read_1pl.
one bwx12 process with the sequence oldread, read, asmread (cfwd) or asmread, read, oldread (crev).
the part L line, started from an idle machine, twice. It was added after the first numbers were seen. It is not part of the plan fixed before the run.
the build script of bwx12. It ran on CRB. It compiled bwx12.c, ran the self-test and wrote this file, build.txt and offsets.tsv.
the tool that prints the machine instructions of a binary file as text.
the C compiler that built bwx12.

gcc flags. `-O3` is optimisation level 3. With `-march=native` gcc picks the instruction set of the machine that it runs on. `-pthread` links the thread library. `-Wall` and `-Wextra` enable warnings. `-std=gnu11` selects the C language of 2011 with GNU extensions [Ref18].
a gcc flag. With it gcc does not replace a loop by a call of a library function such as `memset` [Ref18].

gcc flags. With `-fno-ipa-icf` gcc does not merge two functions that have the same code. With `-fno-toplevel-reorder` gcc keeps the functions in the order of the source file. With `-falign-functions=4` gcc aligns the start of a function to 4 bytes only [Ref18]. bwx12.c needs the last two flags to put each kernel at a chosen address modulo 64 [Ref15].
the option of bwx12 that names the kernels to time, in their order.
one run of the instructions of the loop, from the loop start to the branch that jumps back.
the address of the first instruction of the loop, modulo 64. It is the place of the loop start inside a block of 64 bytes of code addresses.
B is a byte. 1 MiB is 1048576 bytes.
a block of 64 bytes of memory that starts at an address that is a multiple of 64. The comments of bwx12.c use the word "line" for the block that a cache loads as one piece.
one call of the kernel over the whole buffer before the timed interval starts. Its time is not measured.
two more files that build12.sh wrote in the same run. build.txt holds the compiler, the flags and sha256 values. offsets.tsv holds the start address and the loop start of each kernel.
the script that accepts or rejects a build of bwx12. It reads this file and offsets.tsv.
the driver scripts of the whole-chip test of 2026-11-17. go2.sh ran control I.
the general registers of a 64-bit Arm CPU (64 bits each) and the stack pointer. `x0` and `x1` carry the first and the second argument of a function. `x0` carries the return value.
the 32 vector registers of a 64-bit Arm CPU (128 bits each). `qN` names all 16 bytes of register N. `dN` names its low 8 bytes. `vN.2d` names it as two elements of 64 bits.
Arm instructions. `ldp` loads two registers from memory, `ldr` loads one. `stp` stores two registers to memory, `str` stores one.
the instruction "no operation". It changes no register and no memory.
a compare that treats both values as numbers without a sign, as addresses are.
the calling convention of 64-bit Arm: the rules that say which registers carry arguments and which registers must hold their old values when a function returns.

an asm statement is assembler text inside C source. The compiler copies it into the machine code. A macro is a text pattern of the C preprocessor. `DEF_ASMREAD(name, nops)` expands to one kernel function.
a value that compiled code copies to the stack at the start of a function and compares before the return. A changed copy means that the function wrote outside its stack variables.
the registers `x29` and `x30`. `x29` points to the stack area of the current function. `x30` holds the address at which the caller continues.
the first write to newly allocated memory. Linux assigns the physical pages at that moment.
a checksum of 64 hexadecimal digits. Equal values mean equal file content.

refs.what: lines 57 to 65: the loop that wrote this file. For each name that `bwx12 --list` prints it writes the header line and the output of `objdump -d --no-show-raw-insn --disassemble=k_<name>`. With these options objdump prints the instructions of one function, `k_<name>`, without the bytes of each instruction. A filter (the text tool `sed`) keeps only the lines from the function line to the next empty line.
lines 493 to 528: the C source of `k_read`. The loop is lines 505 to 527 (16 loads, the empty asm statement, `p += 32`, the loop test).

lines 168 to 183: the comment on the C kernels. It says that the empty asm statement keeps gcc from deleting the loads of `k_read` and adds no instruction. Lines 286 to 293: the comment on the asm kernels. It says that the compiler cannot add arithmetic, reorder or drop anything in the asm block of the loop. The comment of `k_read` in bwx12.c (lines 493 to 499) points to it under the name bench/bandwidth.c. On 2026-11-21 the file bench/bandwidth.c of the repository and this file had the same sha256 value. That value starts with f1985072. The file of Ref14 records another sha256 value for bandwidth.c in its run. That other value starts with c1406e02. The two texts differ in comment lines only. An edit of 2026-11-13 18:32:07 UTC replaced 2 comment lines above `k_read` with the 5 comment lines 178 to 182 of the local text. The record of the Claude Code session of that day holds the edit (`/home/jhan/.claude/projects/-home-jhan-workspace-titan-cache-perf-crb/7663f0d2-7d09-4571-b80c-92526358fa86.jsonl`, line 1000). With this edit reversed, the local text has the sha256 value of the earlier text (c1406e02...). No code line differs. None exists under /home/jhan/workspace/titan/cache-perf. A later run of 2026-11-13 built the binaries again. Its record holds the value that starts with f1985072 for bandwidth.c [Ref17]. It holds the same sha256 value for the binary bw_new as the file of Ref14. So both texts compiled to the same binary bw_new.
